Juvenile Bicolour parrotfish, Cetoscarus bicolor, settle on Indo-Pacific coral reefs after a pelagic larval phase, and the size at which this transition occurs is a critical life-history bottleneck. The total length at which individuals first attain puberty has been documented at 30 centimeters [Lp = 30 centimeters], a measurement that corresponds roughly to the onset of gonadal recrudescence and the initial development of male-like coloration in this protogynous hermaphrodite. The estimated wet weight at this pubertal stage is 347.4 grams [Wwp = 347.4 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions specific to the species. This size threshold is remarkably consistent across the species' range, suggesting a strong genetic or physiological constraint on the timing of reproductive maturation, though local environmental conditions, particularly food availability, can modulate the age at which this milestone is reached.

As adults, Bicolour parrotfish continue to grow, albeit at a decelerating rate, eventually approaching an asymptotic body size. The ultimate total length for this species has been estimated at 50 centimeters [Li = 50 centimeters], a value typical of a medium-sized scarine labrid. The corresponding ultimate wet weight at this asymptotic length is approximately 1600 grams [Wwi = approximately 1600 grams], representing the maximum body mass an individual is expected to achieve under favourable conditions. This size dimorphism is less pronounced than in some congeneric species, but large terminal-phase males can dominate feeding territories on the reef crest. The transition from initial to terminal phase involves not only a change in colouration but also a fundamental shift in social and reproductive behaviour, with larger individuals controlling access to prime grazing areas.

The initial stages of life are defined by a very small body size at the point of larval settlement and metamorphosis. The wet weight at birth, more accurately described as the mass of the newly settled juvenile following the pelagic larval duration, is estimated at 0.00023 grams [Wwb = 0.00023 grams]. This extraordinarily low mass, roughly equivalent to a small grain of sand, reflects the tiny size of the pelagic egg and the subsequent lecithotrophic larval phase before the onset of exogenous feeding. The yolk-sac larva relies entirely on endogenous reserves until the mouth opens and the individual can begin to capture planktonic prey. This period of high vulnerability is a major source of mortality, with only a tiny fraction of settling larvae surviving to the juvenile stage.

Reproductive investment in this species, like many other parrotfishes, is characterised by batch spawning over an extended breeding season. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) was estimated at approximately 12% [GSI = approximately 12%] at a water temperature of 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C]. This value is typical for a multiple-spawning fish that allocates a moderate proportion of its somatic energy to gamete production each season. Under these thermal conditions, field observations suggest that individual females may participate in up to three separate spawning events per year, releasing buoyant eggs into the water column during lunar-tidal cycles.

The complete life span of Cetoscarus bicolor, from settlement to natural death, has been estimated from otolith increment analysis. The maximum recorded longevity for the species is 4745 days [am = 4745 days], a duration that was determined from individuals collected in the Great Barrier Reef at an ambient water temperature of 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C]. This lifespan is moderate for a scarine labrid, placing it between shorter-lived species such as Scarus psittacus and longer-lived species like Bolbometopon muricatum. The relationship between temperature and longevity is likely mediated through metabolic rate, with higher temperatures generally accelerating somatic growth but potentially shortening the total life span through increased oxidative stress and cellular turnover. This species inhabits coral reef environments across the Indo-Pacific region, where it plays a key ecological role in bioerosion and algal grazing. The complex social structure of this protogynous hermaphrodite, wherein larger terminal-phase males maintain harems of initial-phase females, influences population dynamics and reproductive output across the reef system. Ongoing monitoring of size distributions and spawning aggregations continues to refine understanding of these life-history parameters in relation to environmental variability and fishing pressure.
